# Email Craft · Purely Personal Reference
# by Daniel Paul · Purely Personal

House method for list emails. Distilled from years of coach-and-consultant
email practice. Everything here is described by what it does, not who taught it.

---

## THE HOUSE PHILOSOPHY

- Email is a one-to-one conversation. Write to one person, never "everyone".
- Result before story. Lead with the outcome, then earn it with the details.
- One idea. One email. One CTA. Two asks means neither happens.
- One sentence per paragraph is the default rhythm. White space is deliberate.
- The PS is the second most-read line after the subject. Never waste it.
- Real people, real numbers, real situations. Vague claims burn trust.
- Invite, never sell. Frame every offer as an experience or a next step.
- No warmup lines. "Hope you're well" is a delete-trigger, not a courtesy.

---

## THE EMAIL TYPES (weekly newsletter context)

### 1. The Win-Story Email
Social proof as narrative. Opens with the result, rewinds to the before,
names the exact moves that closed the gap, lands on the after. 100 to 150
words. Soft CTA only.

Shape: result first, then before-state with a specific number, then the stuck
period, then exactly three actions listed one per line without bullets, then
the after-state with a number and a momentum line, then a low-pressure invite.

Example (coach audience):
Subject: From 2 clients to a full roster
"I just heard from a leadership coach who filled her practice this quarter.
When we started, she had 2 clients and a referral pipeline that had gone quiet.
She'd been stuck there for over a year.
She narrowed her offer to one outcome for one type of leader.
Rebuilt her intro call around that outcome.
And started sharing one client result a week with her list.
Now she has 11 clients, a short waitlist, and referrals coming in unprompted.
If you want help doing the same, hit reply with ROSTER and I'll send you the plan we used.
[SIGN-OFF]"

### 2. The Story-First Email
Trust through narrative. Opens mid-scene, builds one beat per paragraph,
plants a mid-story curiosity line ("Why am I telling you this? Stay with me."),
lands the punchline, extracts the lesson in one sentence, then bridges to one
next step. 300 to 500 words. The reader must want the next line at every line.

Example opening (consultant audience):
"The client folded his laptop shut halfway through my pitch.
Not angrily. Worse. Politely."

### 3. The Teach-One-Thing Email
Authority through usefulness. References something you told them before
(continuity builds trust), names one framework, explains it plainly, shows
your personal tweak, then proves you use it ("I run this every Monday.
Without fail."). One CTA at the end. 200 to 350 words.

### 4. The One-Line Curiosity Email
Reactivation through brevity. The subject is just their first name. The body
is a single question, 9 to 15 words, and a sign-off. Nothing else. No pitch,
no context, no links. The shortness is the strategy: it reads like a personal
note, so it gets personal replies.

Example (cold list of consultants):
Subject: Sarah
"Are you still working on getting consistent referrals for your practice?
[SIGN-OFF]"

### 5. The Permission-Based Re-Open
For a list that has gone quiet on YOUR side. Owns the silence in one line,
restates who the list is for and what they'll get from now on, and asks for
one tiny action (a reply or a one-word answer) to re-earn the inbox. Under
120 words. Honest beats clever here.

Example (coach audience):
Subject: I owe you an email
"It's been a while since I showed up in your inbox. That's on me.
Quick reset: this list exists for coaches who want clients from their content, and from now on you'll get one short, useful email a week.
If that's still worth your inbox, reply with one word: IN.
If not, no hard feelings, the unsubscribe link below works fine.
[SIGN-OFF]"

### 6. The Short Check-In
Follow-up for non-responders, 1 to 2 sentences, sent in the same thread.
"Still thinking about [the thing]?" plus sign-off. No new subject line needed.

### 7. The Pain-Question Invite
Fills a live event from a warm list. Opens with the pain as a direct question,
validates the feeling, names the 3 things that are usually missing, positions
the event as where they get all three back, promises one tangible walk-away,
then date plus one CTA. 200 to 300 words.

Example opening (consultant audience):
Subject: Has selling started to feel heavy?
"Instead of loving your client calls, does every proposal feel like pushing a rock uphill?"

---

## SUBJECT LINE CRAFT

Short wins. Five words or fewer beats a clever sentence almost every time.
Often the strongest subject is just a name, a number, or a result.

**The five house formulas:**

| Formula | Pattern | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Transformation | "From [X] to [Y] in [time]" | "From 2 clients to full" |
| Emotional moment | A line from inside the story | "He closed the laptop" |
| First name only | "[Name]" | "Sarah" |
| Pain question | Ask the pain directly | "Has selling started to feel heavy?" |
| Framework name | Name the thing you teach | "The Tuesday Test" |

Rules:
- Never over 8 words. Target 5 or fewer.
- No clickbait: the body must pay off the subject within the first two lines.
- The transformation formula needs real numbers or it reads as hype.
- The first-name-only subject is reserved for one-line emails. Using it on a
  long pitch breaks the trust that makes it work.

---

## PS LINE RULES

The PS is mandatory on every full-length email. Treat it as a second subject line.

- Job 1: carry the proof (a link to a result, a testimonial, an agenda).
- Job 2: plant one secondary curiosity hook or urgency signal, never a second pitch.
- The body holds one CTA. The PS may carry a softer second door, never a louder one.
- One-line emails (types 4, 5, 6) get NO PS. Brevity is the whole play there.

---

## CADENCE PRINCIPLES

- A warm weekly list rotates email types. Never send the same shape two weeks
  running: win-story one week, teach-one-thing the next, story-first the third.
- Proof before ask. In any stretch of 4 emails, at least one is a pure win-story
  with a soft CTA, and it lands before any direct invite.
- Reactivation runs on a 7 to 10 day window, not a blast: one-line curiosity
  email, then a short check-in at day 3 or 4, then one empathy-plus-resource
  email at day 7. Anyone who replies exits the sequence and gets a human answer.
- After reactivation, warm the list back up with value-first emails for 3 sends
  before any event invite or offer.

---

## WHEN TO USE WHICH

| Situation | Email type | Length |
|---|---|---|
| Weekly send, have a fresh client result | Win-Story | 100-150 words |
| Weekly send, have a lesson or story | Story-First | 300-500 words |
| Weekly send, have a process to share | Teach-One-Thing | 200-350 words |
| List went quiet on the reader's side | One-Line Curiosity | 9-15 words |
| List went quiet on the sender's side | Permission-Based Re-Open | under 120 words |
| No reply to a one-liner | Short Check-In | 1-2 sentences |
| Filling a live event or workshop | Pain-Question Invite | 200-300 words |

---

## WHAT NEVER GOES IN A HOUSE EMAIL

- Emojis, em dashes, exclamation marks (unless quoting a real person)
- Two CTAs in the body
- Subject lines over 8 words
- "Best regards" or any corporate sign-off: first name only
- Warmup lines of any kind
- Passive voice
- A benefit claim without a number or a named outcome behind it
